name: Representativeness heuristic
statement: Representativeness is a proposed mechanism rather than a finding: people are said to judge probability by resemblance, and the errors it was coined to explain replicate better than it does.
meaning: Kahneman and Tversky proposed that people answer a question about probability by answering a question about similarity instead. Representativeness is the degree to which a case resembles the category it might have come from, or an outcome resembles the process that might have produced it. Resemblance takes no account of how common a category is, how large a sample is, or how reliable the evidence is. Judgements built on it should therefore go wrong in specific ways, and the 1974 review lists them: neglect of prior probabilities, insensitivity to sample size, misconceptions of chance, insensitivity to predictability, the illusion of validity and misconceptions of regression. Three of those errors have their own entries here, under base rate fallacy, conjunction fallacy and gambler's fallacy. What is at issue in this entry is the shared explanation, not any one of the errors.

origin.note: "Subjective Probability: A Judgment of Representativeness" ran eleven problems on birth sequences, sampling distributions and posterior probabilities. The prediction studies followed in Psychological Review in 1973, and Science carried the summary in 1974. Neither the 1972 nor the 1973 paper could be opened during this check, so figures attributed to them here are read off the 1974 review, the 1983 conjunction paper, Kahneman's Nobel lecture, or the two replications.

evidence: The 1974 review sets out the case. Told that a description had been drawn from a group of 70 engineers and 30 lawyers, or from 30 engineers and 70 lawyers, subjects produced much the same probability judgements in both conditions, though Bayes's rule puts the ratio of the odds at 5.44. Given a description written to carry no information, they answered .5 whichever mix they had been told about, having answered .7 and .3 correctly when given no description at all. Asked whether a hospital with about 45 births a day or one with about 15 recorded more days on which over 60% of babies were boys, 21 undergraduates said the larger, 21 said the smaller and 53 said about the same. Asked which sample was stronger evidence about an urn, 4 red of 5 drawn or 12 red of 20, most chose the first, though the correct posterior odds are 8 to 1 and 16 to 1. The direct evidence for the mechanism comes from a different design, in which one group ranks outcomes by how far a person resembles each and another group ranks the same outcomes by probability. Kahneman's Nobel lecture gives a correlation of .97 between the mean representativeness and mean probability rankings for Tom W., against a rank correlation of -.65 between representativeness rankings and estimated base rates. The Linda figures belong to a particular version, and are usually quoted without it. In Tversky and Kahneman's 1983 paper, 88 undergraduates at the University of British Columbia ranked eight statements about Linda by resemblance, and 85% produced the order feminist, feminist bank teller, bank teller. Other groups ranked the same eight statements by probability. Violations of the conjunction rule ran at 89% among the statistically naive, 90% among the informed and 85% among the sophisticated, and the correlation between mean probability and mean representativeness ranks was .98 for Linda. Kahneman's lecture reports that correlation as .99 and pairs 85% with 89%, which takes the probability figure from the naive group alone.

replication.headline: The chance and sampling problems of 1972 repeat almost intact, eight of nine in a preregistered replication, while the prediction studies of 1973 come apart, with two of six supported.
replication.detail: Mayiwar, Wan, Løhre and Feldman ran the first direct replication of the 1972 paper, on 623 participants, from 683 recruited on Amazon MTurk through CloudResearch, each answering five of the nine problems. Eight of the nine came out as the original did. Of the 343 who saw the birth sequences, 293 rated BGBBBB less probable than GBGBBG, h = 0.79, 95% CI [0.68, 0.89], and 303 rated BBBGGG less probable than GBBGBG, h = 0.87, 95% CI [0.77, 0.98]. Of the 360 who saw the high-school problem, 336 chose the class whose proportions matched the population, h = 1.05, 95% CI [0.95, 1.15]. Of the 348 who saw the randomness problem, 223 called a non-uniform distribution more probable than a uniform one, h = 0.29, 95% CI [0.18, 0.39]. The paper's running text puts all three denominators at 343 and prints the last effect as h = 0.28 with the interval from the birth sequences, so the figures here are taken from its design, descriptives and comparison tables. Estimated sampling distributions did not differ between samples of 10, 100 and 1,000 in any of three scenarios. The one failure was the binomial posterior-probability problem, where the original ordering of judgements did not reappear, though the 5:1 sample still drew the highest subjective probability of coming from the target population while the 40:20 sample was the stronger evidence. On the sample-size problems the authors note that "equally likely" was the modal answer in three of six comparisons rather than five, and that in the best condition 86 of 173 participants chose correctly. The 1973 paper fared worse. Chan, supervised by Feldman, put its studies to 801 US participants on Prolific. Two of the six were supported, two mixed and two not. The engineer-lawyer study was one of the failures. The base-rate manipulation produced a main effect of F(1, 789) = 102.77, p < .001, eta-squared = .081, and the description written to be worthless drew a mean of 64.27% in the high-engineer condition against 32.65% in the low, which is base-rate use rather than base-rate neglect. The outcome-ranking design weakened too. Across six descriptions the replication obtained similarity-probability correlations of .75, .55, .08, .01, -.16 and -.28, only the first of which reached significance, against original values of .88 to .97 that are quoted from the replication's own comparison table rather than from the 1973 paper.

study.cite: Mayiwar, L., Wan, K. H., Løhre, E., & Feldman, G. (2025). Revisiting representativeness heuristic classic paradigms: Replication and extensions of nine experiments in Kahneman and Tversky (1972). Quarterly Journal of Experimental Psychology, 78(4), 707-730.

limits: No multi-site or multi-laboratory replication was located. Searches of Crossref, PubMed, the Open Science Framework, arXiv and the Many Labs and Registered Replication Report catalogues turned up none, so the record is two single-sample online studies. Both originals stayed shut. The 1972 and 1973 papers could not be opened during this check, and the 1974 review was read in the version hosted by the University of California, Irvine. The 1973 replication is the weaker of the two documents. It was read as an undergraduate thesis posted on the Open Science Framework, next to the Stage 1 registered report that Rima-Maria Rahal recommended for in-principle acceptance at Peer Community in Registered Reports on 31 May 2024. That Stage 1 report is listed at N = 1,309, and its own participants section says the 1,309 cases were simulated in Qualtrics and would be replaced by real data at a sample of 800. The real data are in the thesis, at 801. No Stage 2 report was located: the Peer Community site refuses automated requests, Crossref carries one recommendation for this project and no later one, and the project's OSF storage holds a Stage 1 folder and a thesis folder and nothing else. Its item-level correlations each rest on nine fields of specialisation, with seven degrees of freedom, and the intervals printed for them include [-.80, .47] and [-.66, .67]. Ranges that wide settle neither the presence nor the absence of the original correlation. Both replications test the errors rather than the mechanism. No study was found that pits resemblance against a competing account of the same judgements in the same sample.
misreadings: The commonest error is to treat representativeness as a result. It is an explanation, it has been disputed for thirty years, and the errors it explains have mostly held while it has not. Gigerenzer's charge in 1996 was that notions such as representativeness "remain vague, undefined, and unspecified" as to what elicits them and what processes underlie them, and that post hoc one of them can be fitted to almost any experimental result. Kahneman and Tversky replied in the same issue that representativeness can be assessed experimentally and so need not be defined a priori, and that the outcome-ranking evidence had not been challenged. Kahneman later granted in his Nobel lecture that the 1974 article contained no definition of a judgemental heuristic, and that heuristics had been described at various times as principles, as processes, or as sources of cues. He and Frederick supplied one in 2002, attribute substitution, under which a person assesses a hard target attribute by substituting an easier attribute that comes to mind more readily. The outcome-ranking evidence has since been challenged, by the 1973 replication above. The second error is reading base-rate neglect as total. Koehler's review, whose abstract names the lawyer-engineer problem among the evidence, concluded that base rates are almost always used and that how much depends on task structure and representation. The base rate fallacy entry carries the figures. The third is taking the conjunction fallacy and the gambler's fallacy as tests of representativeness. Each has its own entry and its own replication record, and each survives accounts that make no use of resemblance. Barbey and Sloman argue for one such account, that judgements go wrong when a problem obscures the nested sets it contains, and report that almost nobody commits the conjunction fallacy when the options are drawn as Euler circles. The fourth is quoting the 1978 medical study as settled fact about doctors. Barbey and Sloman put its proportion of Bayesian answers at 18%, against 5% for Eddy's mammography problem, and the base rate fallacy entry records how few people it tested.

Source of the eight-statement Linda rankings, the 85%, 89%, 90% and 85% figures and the .98 correlation. Read in the copy hosted at https://pages.ucsd.edu/~cmckenzie/TverskyKahneman1983PsychRev.pdf.
